file_name: Tran-Nguyen K - 2022 - Mobile App Prototype in Older Adults for Postfracture Acute Pain Management User Centered Design App.txt

barriers.description: All study activities were conducted remotely due to COVID-19 restrictions, which may have altered participant interactions with the prototype and limited designers' ability to observe natural use.
barriers.justification: Remote-only data collection constrained the team's ability to understand real-world contexts of use and to evaluate designs under typical conditions, hindering the workloads of understanding context of use and evaluating designs.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Our studies were conducted remotely owing to the COVID-19 pandemic restrictions, which may have affected the participants’ interactions with the prototype.

barriers.description: Usability testing relied on a desktop mobile-device emulator rather than testing on actual smartphones, reducing fidelity of interaction data.
barriers.justification: Using an emulator limited the team's ability to detect usability problems specific to real mobile use, impeding evaluation of designs and understanding context of use needed for iteration.
barriers.reference_excerpt: We used only an emulator on a desktop computer to test our medium-fidelity mHealth prototype; thus, it is possible that some usability problems were not detected. In the future, the prototype should be tested on a smartphone to approximate real use conditions.

barriers.description: Convenience sampling recruited participants with prior exposure to bone-health studies or clinic care, biasing the participant pool toward more informed users.
barriers.justification: This recruitment bias limited the designers' ability to manage a representative, evolving understanding of diverse users and to facilitate involvement of less informed users, affecting the workloads of managing user understanding and facilitating user involvement.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Second, convenience sampling may have biased our results, as we recruited participants who had participated in previous studies on bone health or who had been evaluated in orthopedic clinics at our center. Design workshop participants were well aware of osteoporosis and its negative impacts and may have had prior knowledge related to injury management.

barriers.description: The usability protocol required participants to have Zoom and a computer, which selected for participants with higher technological literacy.
barriers.justification: This inclusion requirement constrained participation of low-tech users and hindered designers' ability to understand and evaluate the app for less tech-literate segments, affecting understanding context of use and facilitating user involvement.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Third, the protocol for the usability tests required participants to have access to Zoom. Consequently, these participants likely had higher technological literacy than those who would never have used videoconferencing tools.

barriers.description: Some participants skipped tutorial pop-ups because they were too long or insufficiently motivating, reducing engagement with onboarding content.
barriers.justification: Participant disengagement with tutorials impeded designers' ability to ensure users learned key interactions and to evaluate comprehension, limiting efforts to integrate feedback and evaluate designs accurately.
barriers.reference_excerpt: As the participants navigated to access different functionalities of our app, tutorials appeared as pop-ups on how to use the functionality. A few participants skipped some of the tutorials and noted that they were too long.

barriers.description: High cognitive load and poorly phrased questions caused participants to omit or enter incorrect information, and many struggled to recall medication names and dosages during testing.
barriers.justification: These user cognitive limitations and question formulation issues limited the designers' ability to evaluate data-entry interactions and to specify robust user requirements for input fields and workflows.
barriers.reference_excerpt: In addition, most participants had trouble remembering which medications and dosages they were prescribed when the app asked them to input their prescriptions. Some questions in the app were poorly formulated; for example, participants expressed confusion over a question in the profile setup, which asked, “Were you prescribed or recommended to take acetaminophen for your pain?”
